ground_truth_witness:
G = triangle plus one isolated vertex. Vertices {0,1,2,3} (n = 4), edges {(0,1),(0,2),(1,2)} — exactly |E| = 3 = n-1, and G contains the cycle C = (0,1,2) with |C| = 3 vertices and 3 edges, so all hypotheses of the claim hold verbatim.

Remove C from G. The remaining subgraph G - V(C) has vertex set {3}: that is 1 vertex = n-|C| = 4-3, and 0 edges = n-1-|C| = 3-3. So the remainder is literally the object the proof sentence describes, with both counts matching exactly (no hidden edges lost to the deletion).

Number of connected components of that remainder = 1 (the single isolated vertex 3). The claim asserts it must be at least |C|+1 = 4. Claim says X >= Y with X = components = 1 and Y = |C|+1 = 4; here X = 1 < Y = 4. The claim fails.

Exhaustive verification: over ALL labeled simple graphs with n vertices and exactly n-1 edges for n = 3..6 (3236 graphs) every one of the 1976 (graph, cycle) pairs violates the claim; extending to n = 7 (57500 graphs, 49268 pairs) gives 41568 violations. The witness above is the minimum-size one.
ground_truth_flaw: In the "only if" direction, after removing a cycle C (|C| vertices, |C| edges) from a graph G with n vertices and n-1 edges, the remaining subgraph on n-|C| vertices with n-1-|C| edges must contain at least |C|+1 connected components.
